new_statements.quote: Li accentu primari sta sur li vocal ante li ultim consonant, ma ne sur li quar síllabes bil, ic, im, ul, queles porta li accentu al precedent síllab, mem si ti-ci es bil, ic, im, ul. Un simplic s e li du síllabes men e um in li fine del parol ne changea li accentuation del precedent parol-parte. Si ti regules ne es aplicabil, on accentua li prim vocal del parol. Si li natural accentuation ne seque ti regul, it es marcat per un accentu scrit (preferibilmen quam in é, tolerat anc è o ê). [...] In parol-compositiones (anc autonom paroles con prefixes) li principal parte seque ti regules, li altres posse reciver un accentu secundari.
new_statements.translation: The primary stress is on the vowel before the last consonant, but not on the four syllables bil, ic, im, ul, which take the accent on the preceding syllable, even if this is bil, ic, im, ul. A simple s and the two syllables men and um at the end of the word do not change the stress of the preceding part of the word. If those rules are not applicable, one stresses the first vowel of the word. If the natural stress does not follow this rule, it is marked by a written accent (preferably as in é, also tolerated are è or ê). [...] In composed words (also standalone words with prefixes) the first part follows these rules, the others may receive a secondary accent. (translation as in the pbworks English version of Haas 1956, § 8)
new_statements.citation: Haas, Fritz. 1956. Grammatica de Interlingue in Interlingue. Winterthur (Svissia): Interlingue-Servicie. Digitalisat de S. Belitzky (via the Internet Archive 2021-02-11 of panix.com/~bartlett/). Section ACCENTUATION, § 8. English rendering from the same work's English translation (HTML adaptation S. Hartwig 2009, interlingue.pbworks.com, the Internet Archive 2013), section STRESS § 8.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Opened (header: 'Dr. F. Haas, Grammatica de Interlingue in Interlingue, Digitalisat de S. Belitzky ex edition de Interlingue-Servicie Winterthur (Svissia) 1956', preface signed 'Dr. phil. Fritz Haas', Winterthur, octobre 1956). Section ACCENTUATION begins at the text layer, '§ 8.' at line 268. Lines 269-293 read, modulo the digitization's line breaks: 'Li accentu primari sta sur li vocal ante li ultim consonant, ma ne sur li quar síllabes bil, ic, im, ul, queles porta li accentu al precedent síllab, mem si ti-ci es bil, ic, im, ul. Un simplic s e li du síllabes men e um in li fine del parol ne changea li accentuation del precedent parol-parte. Si ti regules…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress the vowel that precedes the word's last consonant: consonant-final words are stressed on the final syllable (doctór, formár, parol), vowel-final words on the penult (fórme, famílie, státue). Four adjectival/nominal suffixes -bil, -ic, -im, -ul are extrametrical and throw stress one syllable back (possíbil, lógic, últim, régul), and so are the plural -s and the endings -men, -um (rapídmen, máximum). Words with no vowel before the last consonant (die, deo) stress the first vowel. Everything else is lexical and must be written with an accent (café, numeró, númere, bontá). Provisional code 'weight-sensitive' because the position is decided by whether the final syllable is closed (closed final = stressed, else penult), within a two-syllable window; an alternative code is 'fixed: other position' (position defined by the last consonant). The 1929 Complet Grammatica (Janotta, Cosmoglotta 65, pp. 165-167) states the same rule in the same form and is the earliest official statement found.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Haas § 8: in compounds and prefixed words the main part follows the rule and the other parts 'may receive a secondary accent'. Janotta 1929 point 5 is more explicit: each member of a compound may carry stress; a determinative noun/adjective or the negative prefix in- takes primary stress and the particle takes none or secondary (férrovía, málhumorát, rétrovenír); -men adverbs may carry secondary stress on -men.
new_statements.exceptions: Suffixes -bil, -ic, -im, -ul unstressed (stress retracted); plural -s, -men, -um do not affect stress; words with no vowel before the final consonant (die, deo, tui, via) stress the first vowel; all other deviations are lexical and carry a written acute (café, qualitá, numeró, ómine, númere, amíc); Haas § 9: in fluent speech only the most important words of the phrase are stressed, and an emphatic accent may override the rule (medicó vs médico); the written accent may be omitted on frequent words.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, orthographically defined rule for a constructed language (the rule is stated over letters, 'vowel before the last consonant'); Haas § 9 adds a phrase-level remark that connected speech stresses only the important words. No instrumental or spoken-corpus evidence exists; all sources are prescriptive grammars/courses.
new_statements.identity_note: inte1262 'Interlingue' is a Glottolog duplicate of inte1260 'Interlingue (Occidental)' [ISO 639-3 ile]: one constructed language, published by Edgar de Wahl in Kosmoglott (Reval/Tallinn, Estonia — hence country EE) in 1922 as Occidental and renamed Interlingue in 1949. Glottolog 5.3 attaches no references to inte1262. All sources read describe the single standard variety (there are no dialects); the 1929 Complet Grammatica uses the name Occidental, Haas 1956 the name Interlingue. A sibling folder holds copies of the same Haas and Cosmoglotta sources; the two keys should be merged into one catalog entry.

new_statements.quote: 1. Li accentu tonic es situat ordinarmen sur li vocal ante li ultim consonant. In li exemples secuent li accentu es indicat per grass lítteres [...]: crater, doctor, [...] colere, farine, honore, [...] linea, Austria, [...] familie, [...] statue; felici, [...] 2. Li finales -bil, -ic, (si it es pronunciat [ik]), -im, -ul es ínaccentuat e attrae li accentu al precendent syllabe, mem si li precedent syllabe es un de ti quar syllabes (finales atonic); labil, nobil, possibil, stabil; [...] 3. Li finale -s del plurale e li finales -men e -um es ínaccentuat e ne have influentie al accentu del céteri parol-parte (finales enclitic)
new_statements.translation: 1. The tonic accent is normally situated on the vowel before the last consonant. In the following examples the accent is indicated by bold letters [...]: crater, doctor, [...] colere, farine, honore, [...] linea, Austria, [...] familie, [...] statue; felici, [...] 2. The endings -bil, -ic (if pronounced [ik]), -im, -ul are unstressed and draw the accent onto the preceding syllable, even if the preceding syllable is one of these four syllables (atonic endings); labil, nobil, possibil, stabil; [...] 3. The plural ending -s and the endings -men and -um are unstressed and have no influence on the accent of the rest of the word (enclitic endings).

new_statements.relation_note: Same rule as the existing statement (Haas 1956 § 8: 'accentu primari sta sur li vocal ante li ultim consonant', with the four atonic endings bil, ic, im, ul and the enclitic s, men, um). This 1929 Complet Grammatica is the earlier, more detailed source of that rule; it adds the first-vowel rule for vowel-only words, the compound/secondary-accent rules and the explicit list of graphic-accent exceptions. It describes Occidental (renamed Interlingue 1949), i.e. the same language.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the vowel before the last consonant of the word: final syllable if the word ends in a consonant (doctór, generál), penult if it ends in one vowel (farína, colére), antepenult if it ends in two vowels (famílie, Austria). The endings -bil, -ic, -im, -ul are unstressed and throw stress one syllable back; plural -s and the endings -men, -um are enclitic and do not move the stress. Words with no vowel before the last consonant (die, deo, noi) stress the first vowel (point 4, p. 166). Words not conforming carry a written acute accent (bontá, café, numeró, ábdomin, cétere; point 6, p. 166).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Point 5 (p. 166): in compounds each part may carry a tonic accent by the rules above; if the first (determining) part is a noun, adjective or the negative prefix in-, it takes the primary accent (férrovía, málhumorát, inpracticábil); if it is a particle it takes no accent or an accessory (secondary) accent and the second part takes the primary (rétrovenír, ápplicár, cóntradír). Adverbial -men, being an abbreviated 'mente', may take a secondary accent (respectabilmen, sobrimen; point 3).
new_statements.exceptions: Points 2-3: unstressed suffixes -bil, -ic, -im, -ul (labil, hyperbolic, ultim, vocabul) and enclitic -s, -men, -um; point 4: monosyllabic-vowel words stress the first vowel; point 6: all other non-conforming words are written with a graphic accent (bontá, mamá, qualitá, allé, café, idé, moné, societé, buró, numeró, menú, cacáo, muséo, ábdomin, ómine, órdine, término, cétere, éther, númere, hypérbol, límite, and, contrary to points 2-3, amíc, formíca, íntim, sublím, parfúm, Haití, país); points 7-9: the graphic accent may be omitted in frequent words, may mark homonyms (te/té, si/sí) and rhetorical stress on monosyllables; points 10-11: warnings to Germans (doctór, motór, stabil, mobil) and French speakers (-ic words).
new_statements.identity_note: The work describes Occidental (Edgar de Wahl's language, renamed Interlingue in 1949) as codified by the Occidental-Academie in 1929; inte1262 is a Glottolog duplicate of inte1260 Interlingue/Occidental [ile], with no dialectal variety involved.

sources.note: 'Generalmen li accentu sta sur li vocale ante li ultim consonant, ma it es self-evident que li finition -s ne have influentie. Anc li finitiones -bil, -ic, -im, -ul, -men es presc sempre inaccentuat in li vocabularium international. Si un parol have un accentu exter ti du regules, on indica su plazza per un signe (accentu scrit).' Also states the design principle that the language keeps the natural stress of international words 'mem si it ne es uniform'.
